title: Finite Galois descent for commutative Hopf algebras
statement: Let $L/k$ be a finite Galois extension of fields [def-weil-field, def-pc-field-extension]: $\dim_kL<\infty$, $L/k$ is separable algebraic [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension], and $L/k$ is normal (for every $\alpha\in L$ the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $k$ is a product of polynomials of degree one in $L[T]$). Let $\Pi=\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)$ be the group of field automorphisms of $L$ fixing $k$ pointwise. A commutative Hopf $L$-algebra is a commutative $L$-algebra $B$ with algebra maps $\Delta:B\to B\otimes B$, $\epsilon:B\to L$ and an antipode $S:B\to B$ satisfying the coassociativity, counit and inverse identities displayed in [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. A semilinear $\Pi$-action on $B$ consists of additive multiplicative bijections $\sigma_B$ satisfying the group-action identities and $\sigma_B(\lambda b)=\sigma(\lambda)\sigma_B(b)$, satisfying $\sigma_B S=S\sigma_B$, $\epsilon(\sigma_B b)=\sigma(\epsilon(b))$, and $\Delta\sigma_B=(\sigma_B\otimes\sigma_B)\Delta$ under the diagonal semilinear action on $B\otimes_L B$. Scalar extension $A\mapsto L\otimes_k A$, with action $\sigma(\lambda\otimes a)=\sigma(\lambda)\otimes a$, is an equivalence from commutative Hopf $k$-algebras to commutative Hopf $L$-algebras with semilinear $\Pi$-action; morphisms in the latter category are $L$-linear Hopf maps commuting with the action. Its quasi-inverse is the invariant algebra $B^\Pi$, with descended Hopf operations. The counit is the natural Hopf isomorphism $L\otimes_k B^\Pi\to B$, $\lambda\otimes b\mapsto\lambda b$, and the unit is $A\to(L\otimes_k A)^\Pi$, $a\mapsto1\otimes a$. This equivalence restricts to finitely generated algebras [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]. Tensor products have the meaning in [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property].

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, including its Hopf-algebra consequence; A.66, p.581, for descent of morphisms. Finite-generation restriction by descent of a finite set of algebra generators.

proof.text: Put $A=B^\Pi$. Additivity and multiplicativity of the action make $A$ a commutative $k$-subalgebra. Vector-space descent gives an equivariant linear isomorphism $\theta:L\otimes_k A\to B$. It is an algebra map: on pure tensors $\theta((\lambda\otimes a)(\mu\otimes a'))=\lambda\mu aa'=\theta(\lambda\otimes a)\theta(\mu\otimes a')$, and it sends $1\otimes1$ to $1$. Thus it is an algebra isomorphism. The unit of vector-space descent for $U=k$, followed by $L\otimes_k k\simeq L$, identifies $L^\Pi$ with $k$.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, vector-space descent and its Hopf-algebra consequence; details of the consequence supplied here.

proof.text:
For $n=2,3$, iteration of tensor base change gives an isomorphism
$$\rho_n:L\otimes_k A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow B^{\otimes_L n},\quad \lambda\otimes(a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n)\longmapsto\lambda a_1\otimes a_2\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n.$$
Here first switch the scalar factor using $x\otimes\lambda\leftrightarrow\lambda\otimes x$ and then apply the cited base-change isomorphism and $\theta$ to each factor. The displayed formula makes $\rho_n$ equivariant; multiplication of pure tensors makes it an algebra isomorphism. Apply $\eta$ of vector-space descent to $U=A^{\otimes_k n}$, then take invariants of $\rho_n$. This gives an algebra isomorphism
$$\chi_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\xrightarrow{\sim}(B^{\otimes_L n})^\Pi,\quad a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n\mapsto a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n.$$
No assertion that invariants commute with arbitrary tensor products is assumed; these particular comparisons follow from $\rho_n$ and the stated unit isomorphism.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, vector-space descent and its Hopf-algebra consequence; details of the consequence supplied here.

proof.text: For $a\in A$, equivariance gives $\Delta_B(a)\in(B\otimes_L B)^\Pi$, $\epsilon_B(a)\in L^\Pi=k$, and $S_B(a)\in A$. Define $\Delta_A(a)=\chi_2^{-1}(\Delta_B(a))$, $\epsilon_A(a)=\epsilon_B(a)$ in $k$, and $S_A(a)=S_B(a)$. Restrictions and the algebra isomorphism $\chi_2$ show that all three are $k$-algebra maps. Under $\theta$ and $\rho_2$, their scalar extensions are exactly $\Delta_B,\epsilon_B,S_B$: on $\lambda\otimes a$ their values become $\lambda\Delta_B(a),\lambda\epsilon_B(a),\lambda S_B(a)$.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, vector-space descent and its Hopf-algebra consequence; details of the consequence supplied here.

proof.text: The coassociativity equation for $\Delta_A$ is an equality of maps $A\to A^{\otimes_k3}$. After extension to $L$ and $\rho_3$ it is exactly $(\Delta_B\otimes1)\Delta_B=(1\otimes\Delta_B)\Delta_B$. The two counit equations similarly become $(\epsilon_B\otimes1)\Delta_B=1_B=(1\otimes\epsilon_B)\Delta_B$ under the tensor unit identifications. Finally the two antipode equations become $\mu_B(S_B\otimes1)\Delta_B=u_B\epsilon_B=\mu_B(1\otimes S_B)\Delta_B$. These identifications follow by the formulas for $\rho_2,\rho_3$ and their naturality in each factor; multiplication maps $a\otimes a'$ to $aa'$ on both sides. Scalar extension is faithful by the Hom bijection in vector-space descent, so each equality holds over $k$. These are precisely the Hopf identities specified in the statement, hence $A$ is a Hopf algebra and $\theta$ a Hopf isomorphism.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, vector-space descent and its Hopf-algebra consequence; details of the consequence supplied here.

proof.text: Conversely, for a commutative Hopf $k$-algebra $C$, give $L\otimes_k C$ its tensor algebra structure. If $\Delta_C(c)=\sum_i c_i\otimes d_i$, set $\Delta_L(\lambda\otimes c)=\sum_i(\lambda\otimes c_i)\otimes_L(1\otimes d_i)$, $\epsilon_L(\lambda\otimes c)=\lambda\epsilon_C(c)$, and $S_L(\lambda\otimes c)=\lambda\otimes S_C(c)$. Tensor base change makes these well-defined algebra maps. On pure tensors the three Hopf identities are exactly those for $C$, multiplied by $\lambda$, so they hold. The action $\sigma(\lambda\otimes c)=\sigma(\lambda)\otimes c$ is additive, multiplicative, semilinear, and satisfies the group law. The same formulas give its compatibility with all three operations, including $\epsilon_L\sigma=\sigma\epsilon_L$. The vector-space unit $\eta_C:c\mapsto1\otimes c$ is an algebra isomorphism onto invariants and respects each displayed operation, hence is a Hopf isomorphism.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, vector-space descent and its Hopf-algebra consequence; details of the consequence supplied here.

proof.text: If $F:B\to B'$ is an equivariant $L$-linear Hopf map, its restriction $F_0:A\to A'$ is a $k$-algebra map. It preserves $\epsilon$ and $S$ by restriction. For comultiplication, apply the injective comparison $\chi'_2$ to the desired equation: both sides become $\Delta_{B'}F(a)=(F\otimes_L F)\Delta_B(a)$. Naturality of the tensor comparison identifies the second side with the image of $(F_0\otimes_k F_0)\Delta_A(a)$. Thus $F_0$ is a Hopf map. Conversely the scalar extension of any Hopf map is a Hopf map by the formulas in the previous step. The identity $F(\lambda a)=\lambda F_0(a)$ shows $F\theta_B=\theta_{B'}(1\otimes F_0)$, so the vector-space Hom bijection restricts to exactly the required bijection on Hopf maps.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, vector-space descent and its Hopf-algebra consequence; details of the consequence supplied here.

proof.text: Restriction to invariants respects identities and compositions, as does scalar extension. The previous formulas prove naturality of $\theta$ and $\eta$ for Hopf maps. The two triangle composites are identities: $L\otimes C\xrightarrow{1\otimes\eta_C}L\otimes(L\otimes C)^\Pi\xrightarrow{\theta_{L\otimes C}}L\otimes C$ sends $\lambda\otimes c$ to $\lambda\otimes c$, and $B^\Pi\xrightarrow{\eta_{B^\Pi}}(L\otimes B^\Pi)^\Pi\xrightarrow{(\theta_B)^\Pi}B^\Pi$ sends $b$ to $b$. These natural Hopf isomorphisms exhibit the two functors as inverse equivalences.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581, vector-space descent and its Hopf-algebra consequence; details of the consequence supplied here.

proof.text: If $C$ is generated over $k$ by $c_1,\ldots,c_r$, then $L\otimes C$ is generated over $L$ by $1\otimes c_i$: every pure tensor is an $L$-multiple of a polynomial in these elements. Conversely suppose $B$ is generated over $L$ by $b_1,\ldots,b_r$. Use $\theta^{-1}$ to write each $b_i$ as a finite sum $\sum_j\lambda_{ij}a_{ij}$ with $a_{ij}\in A$. Let $A_0\subset A$ be the $k$-subalgebra generated by this finite set. Every $L$-polynomial in the $b_i$ belongs to the $L$-linear span of $A_0$, so that span is all of $B$. Let $q:A\to A/A_0$ be the quotient map of $k$-vector spaces (the quotient by the underlying linear subspace, not an algebra quotient). The map $(1\otimes q)\theta^{-1}$ kills $A_0$ and therefore all its $L$-span $B$. Faithfulness of scalar extension gives $q=0$. Hence every $a\in A$ lies in $A_0$, so $A=A_0$ is finitely generated. Together these implications prove the restriction to finitely generated algebras.
